LETTERS TO THE EDITOR 
STIFF-MAN SYNDROME: ABNORMAL 
LATE RESPONSES UPON TRANSCRANIAL 
MAGNETIC STIMULATION 
Stiff-man syndrome (SMS) is a rare disorder characterized 
by fluctuating stiffness of axial and proximal limb muscles. 
The diagnosis is made on clinical signs and symptoms, 
and there is no diagnostic test specific for SMS. We here 
report a SMS patient who showed characteristic abnormal 
late responses upon transcranial magnetic stimulation 
(TMS). 
A 29-year-old woman complained of attacks of painful 
muscle stiffness mostly provoked by emotional stress or 
unexpected events. Thoracic and lumbar paraspinal, ab- 
dominal, and proximal left leg muscles were involved. Dur- 
ing the attacks, which lasted for up to 2 min, the patient 
was unable to walk. Between attacks, there was fluctuating 
rigidity of the involved muscles. An insulin-dependent dia- 
betes mellitus had been diagnosed 15 years before. On 
neurological examination, she fulfilled the criteria' for the 
diagnosis of SMS. Magnetic resonance imaging of the skull 
was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid was normal, but in 1991 
there had been oligoclonal banding. Immunological stud- 
ies showed high titers of autoantibodies against pancreatic 
islet cells. Anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibod- 
ies were positive. Motor and sensory nerve conduction, 
needle electromyography of limb muscles, visual evoked 
potentials, and blink reflex were normal. 
Spasmodic reflex myoclonus, as recently described in 
8 other cases of SMS,' was found only in lumbar and tho- 
racic, and habituating excessive acoustic startle reflex' only 
in the lumbar paraspinal muscles. 
Upon TMS central motor conduction time (CMCT) 
was normal to the hypothenar and anterior tibial muscles. 
Additionally, in the anterior tibial muscles there were late 
responses (LRs) upon cortical (latency 69-70 ms) and lum- 
bar (latency 82-85 ms) stimulation (Fig. la). The ampli- 
tude of the LR in the affected left leg was higher compared 
to the unaffected right leg. The LRs were independent of 
an attack of stiffness and did not habituate. The LRs were 
seen by different examiners on different days. Treatment

In normal subjects the compound rnuscle actiori poten- 
tial elicited by TMS is followed by a silent period that 
terminates at least 80 ms after the stimulus.' Hence, the 
LRs upon cortical stimulation were clearly abnormal. The 
amplitude of the LRs corresponded with the symptoms:

MYASTHENIA GRAVIS AFTER 
INTERFERON=ALPHA TREATMENT 
The primary defect in myasthenia gravis (MG) is an au- 
thoantibody-mediated dysfunction of the acetylcholine re- 
ceptors in the neuromuscular junction. Under rare condi- 
tions this autoantibody production appears to be induced 
by an external stimulus. We report a case of acetylcholine 
receptor antibody-positive myasthenia gravis after inter- 
feron (1FN)-alpha treatment for myelogenous leukemia. 
In a 47-year-old man Philadelphia chromosome- 
positive chronic myelogenous leukemia was diagnosed. 
The patient received recombinant interferon alpha-2b (Es- 
sex Pharma) therapy with 5 X 10' units daily, SC. The 
injections were well tolerated and induced hematological 
remission. 
After 8 months of treatment the patient developed 
generalized edema which was attributed to IFN-alpha and 
treatment was discontinued. After 4 weeks he exhibited 
additional fatigue and progressing paresis of the legs. Uni- 
lateral facial paresis was followed by symmetrical facial mus- 
cle weakness and impaired oculomotor movements. Ten- 
don reflexes were absent but there was no disturbance of 
sensory function. Lumbar cerebrospinal fluid showed a 
slightly elevated protein (49.8 mg/dL) and a normal cell 
count. Diuretics and albumin substitution achieved renal 
recompensation and the neurological symptoms and signs 
also improved. 
After 2 months the patient was readmitted following 
recurrence of renal failure and muscle weakness. In addi- 
tion he had developed dysphagia and marked bilateral 
ptosis and oculomotor function was restricted to slight hori- 
zontal movements. There was proximal pronounced mus- 
cle weakness. All tendon reflexes were absent. Assuming 
the presence of a neuromuscular transmission defect, a 
test dose of edrophoniumchloride 2 mg was administered, 
resulting in dramatically improved muscle strength. In sup- 
port of this finding repetitive electric 3-Hz stimulation of 
the abductor pollicis brevis muscle revealed an abnormal 
decrement of 12% in compound motor action potential 
(CMAF') amplitude. Single-fiber electromyography of the 
extensor digitorum communis muscle (EDC) at all poten- 
tials demonstrated an abnormal jitter frequently accompa- 
nied by transmission blocking. Stimulated single-fiber elec- 
tromyography (EMG) of the EDC ruled out a presynaptic 
defect. Electroneurographic studies showed normal con- 
duction velocities in the upper limbs. Axonopathy was seen 
in the lower limbs with slightly reduced velocities and 
CMAP amplitudes. 
The acetylcholine receptor-antibody titer was increased 
(31 nmol) as well as thyrotropin receptor-antibody and 
thyroglobulin-antibody titers. A mediastinal computerized 
tomography scan was negative for thymoma. The treatment 
of myasthenia gravis with pyridostigmin (360 mg) and pred- 
nison (100 mg) immediately improved muscle strength 
and performance. 
Fatigue, weakness, and neuropathy are frequently ob- 
served adverse reactions in patients treated with IFN alpha- 
2b for chronic myelogenous leukemia.' Our patient devel- 
oped marked weakness and fatigue after 8 months of 
highdose IFN-alpha treatment (5 X lo6 units/day). The 
presence of polyradiculopathy was ruled out. The reduced 
CMAP amplitudes as well as reduced conduction velocities 
and lost reflexes indicate mild neuropathy. Neuropathy, 
however, does not serve to explain the pronounced, activity- 
dependent muscle weakness. 
Two similar cases of myasthenia gravis was postive ace- 
tylcholine-receptor autoantibodies under IFN-alpha ther- 
apy noted in our patient have been reported.' In analogy 
to penicillamine-induced MG we suggest that autoantibody 
production against postsynaptic membrane structures by 
IFN-alpha is the most likely underlying pathophysiology.

INCIDENCE OF CEREBRAL INFARCTION 
IN DUCHENNE MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY 
Cardiomyopathy is one of the most important clinical mani- 
festations in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) .’ One 
third of DMD patients die from cardiac failure. Cerebral 
infarction is a possible complication of DMD cardiomyopa- 
thy, as in the case of idiopathic dilated cardi~myopathf,~; 
however, there has been only one detailed case report4 
and the frequency is considered to be negligibly low.’ To 
determine the incidence of cerebral infarction in DMD we 
sent questionnaires to 25 National Institutions for Muscular 
Dystrophy located throughout Japan, asking the number 
and age distribution of DMD patients, the number of DMD 
patients who had cerebral infarction during the year of 
1993, and the age at the onset of stroke. We received replies 
from 22 institutions and 665 DMD patients were included 
in this study. Five patients had cerebral infarction during 
this period and they were all between 16 and 20 years of 
age as shown in Table 1. Lesion was located in the right 
hemisphere (extensive) in 1 patient, in the right temporo- 
parietal lobe in 2, and in the left frontal lobe in 1. Stroke 
manifested itself as hemiparesis of sudden onset in 4 pa- 
tients and transient motor aphasia in l. All the patients 
showed dilated cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation was 
observed in 1. Autopsy revealed asymptomatic right tempo- 
ral lobe infarction in a cardiomyopathy-free patient (on- 
set unknown). 
Here we conclude that the incidence of cerebral infarc- 
tion is 0.75% for all DMD patients and 1.8% for patients 
between 16 and 20 years of age. Cardiomyopathy is the 
most important predisposing factor. Considering that most 
DMD patients above the age of 16 years show severe muscle 
weakness which may obscure the onset of stroke, the real 
incidence could be much higher, and whether or not to 
start anticoagulation therapy to DMD patients with heart 
failure is an important question.

LARGE MITOCHONDRIAL DNA 
DELETIONS IN MITOCHONDRIAL

encephalomyopathies. In order to detect these mtDNA 
deletions previously, we have to use Southern blotting tech- 
nique and/or several sets of conventional polymerase chain 
reaction (PCR)6 because human mtDNA is 16.6 kb,’ and is, 
therefore, too long to amplify by conventional PCR applied 
with one set of primers. Recently, long PCR, which can 
amplify greater than 10 kb of DNA, was reported.’ ’ We 
applied long PCR for the detection of large mtDXA dele- 
tions in patients with CPEO.

POSTINFECTIOUS DEMYELINATING 
POLYNEUROPATHY MIMICKING 
MYASTHENIA GRAVIS 
Ocular muscles are affected first in about half of the cases 
of myasthenia gravis resulting in fluctuating ptosis and 
diplopia. The fluctuating nature of myasthenic weakness 
is unlikely in any other disorder. The Guillain-BarrC syn- 
drome can cause ocular motor nerve paresis.' 
This report describes a patient who developed fluctuat- 
ing ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, and fatigue mimicking my- 
asthenia gravis in whom the neurophysiological investiga- 
tions showed a demyelinating polyneuropathy and 
increased orbicularis oculi muscle jitter. 
A 47-year-old man was referred for evaluation of bilat- 
eral ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, and fatigue. The patient 
was in excellent health until 2 weeks before, when he had 
fever, muscle tenderness and tiredness for some days. One 
week later he noticed increased tiredness with the custom- 
ary daily activities. Another week later he had diplopia, 
bilateral ptosis, and difficulty chewing and swallowing at 
the end of meals. All these symptoms were clearly improved 
by rest and worsened with prolonged activity and at the 
end of the day. On neurologic examination the patient 
had bilateral ptosis and marked limitation of all ocular 
movements in both eves with normal Dhotomotor reflexes.

tomography scan was negative for thymoma. The treatment 
of myasthenia gravis with pyridostigmin (360 mg) and pred- 
nison (100 mg) immediately improved muscle strength 
and performance. 
Fatigue, weakness, and neuropathy are frequently ob- 
served adverse reactions in patients treated with IFN alpha- 
2b for chronic myelogenous leukemia.' Our patient devel- 
oped marked weakness and fatigue after 8 months of 
highdose IFN-alpha treatment (5 X lo6 units/day). The 
presence of polyradiculopathy was ruled out. The reduced 
CMAP amplitudes as well as reduced conduction velocities 
and lost reflexes indicate mild neuropathy. Neuropathy, 
however, does not serve to explain the pronounced, activity- 
dependent muscle weakness. 
Two similar cases of myasthenia gravis was postive ace- 
tylcholine-receptor autoantibodies under IFN-alpha ther- 
apy noted in our patient have been reported.' In analogy 
to penicillamine-induced MG we suggest that autoantibody 
production against postsynaptic membrane structures by 
IFN-alpha is the most likely underlying pathophysiology.

INCIDENCE OF CEREBRAL INFARCTION 
IN DUCHENNE MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY 
Cardiomyopathy is one of the most important clinical mani- 
festations in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) .’ One 
third of DMD patients die from cardiac failure. Cerebral 
infarction is a possible complication of DMD cardiomyopa- 
thy, as in the case of idiopathic dilated cardi~myopathf,~; 
however, there has been only one detailed case report4 
and the frequency is considered to be negligibly low.’ To 
determine the incidence of cerebral infarction in DMD we 
sent questionnaires to 25 National Institutions for Muscular 
Dystrophy located throughout Japan, asking the number 
and age distribution of DMD patients, the number of DMD 
patients who had cerebral infarction during the year of 
1993, and the age at the onset of stroke. We received replies 
from 22 institutions and 665 DMD patients were included 
in this study. Five patients had cerebral infarction during 
this period and they were all between 16 and 20 years of 
age as shown in Table 1. Lesion was located in the right 
hemisphere (extensive) in 1 patient, in the right temporo- 
parietal lobe in 2, and in the left frontal lobe in 1. Stroke 
manifested itself as hemiparesis of sudden onset in 4 pa- 
tients and transient motor aphasia in l. All the patients 
showed dilated cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation was 
observed in 1. Autopsy revealed asymptomatic right tempo- 
ral lobe infarction in a cardiomyopathy-free patient (on- 
set unknown). 
Here we conclude that the incidence of cerebral infarc- 
tion is 0.75% for all DMD patients and 1.8% for patients 
between 16 and 20 years of age. Cardiomyopathy is the 
most important predisposing factor. Considering that most 
DMD patients above the age of 16 years show severe muscle 
weakness which may obscure the onset of stroke, the real 
incidence could be much higher, and whether or not to 
start anticoagulation therapy to DMD patients with heart 
failure is an important question.

SIMPLE AND RAPID DETECTION OF 
LARGE MITOCHONDRIAL DNA 
DELETIONS IN MITOCHONDRIAL 
ENCEPHALOMYOPATHYBYLONGPCR 
Large mitochondrial (mt) DNA deletions4 are found in 
about two thirds of patients with chronic progressive exter- 
nal opthalmoplegia (CPEO) , including patients with 
Kearns-Sayre syndrome,’ one of the major mitochondrial 
encephalomyopathies. In order to detect these mtDNA 
deletions previously, we have to use Southern blotting tech- 
nique and/or several sets of conventional polymerase chain 
reaction (PCR)6 because human mtDNA is 16.6 kb,’ and is, 
therefore, too long to amplify by conventional PCR applied 
with one set of primers. Recently, long PCR, which can 
amplify greater than 10 kb of DNA, was reported.’ ’ We 
applied long PCR for the detection of large mtDXA dele- 
tions in patients with CPEO. 
DNAwas extracted from control white blood cells (Cl), 
control skeletal muscle (C2), and CPEO patients’ skeletal 
muscles (P1 and P2) by standard methods. The PCK reac- 
tion (50 pL) consisted of 5 pL 1OX LA PCR buffer (Ta- 
kara), 2.5 U Takara Ex Taq (Takara), 250 p mol/L 
each dNTP, 0.25 p mol/L primer A[5’-TGGCCACA 
GCACTTAAACACATCTC-3’, mtDNA 321- 345( l)], 
0.25 p mol/L primer B( 5’-TGCTGTACTTGCTTGTAAG 
CATGGG-3’, mtDNA 16215+16191 (l)], and human DNA 
(50 ng-1 pg). PCR cycles consisted of 1 min at 94°C and 
30 cycles of 20 s at 98°C and 15 min at 68”C, using DNA 
thermal cycler PJ 2000 (Perkin-Elmer) and Ampli WaxTM 
PCR Gem 100 (Perkin-Elmer). PCR 5olution (5-10 pL)

As shown in Figure 1, controls (Cl,C2) showed 15.9- 
kb bands and CPEO patients (Pl,P2) showed 12.3-kb and 
10.9kb bands. These bands were identified as mtDNA by 
Southern blotting, using human placental mtDNA as a 
probe (data not shown). In these patients, deletion sizes, 
proportions, and sites were already determined before long 
PCR by Southern blotting, several sets of conventional PCR, 
and DNA sequencing (Pl, 3.6-kb deletion, 42% deletion 
proportion, deletion site between mtDNA 8639-12208; P2, 
5.0kb deletion, 49% deletion proportion, deletion site be- 
tween mtDNA 8482-13459). The deletion sizes determined 
by long PCR were consistent with the deletion sizes deter- 
mined by Southern blotting or conventional PCR. How- 
ever, in CPEO patients with heteroplasmy of wild and de- 
leted mtDNA, only deleted mtDNA was amplified by long 
PCR. We speculate that smaller mtDNA may be dominant 
over larger mtDNA in this system. Therefore, in this system, 
we could not quantify deleted mtDNA. 
Long PCR provides a simple and rapid procedure to 
identify deleted mtDNA. This procedure can be performed 
within 1 day, cornparedwith approximately 1 week required 
to perform Southern blotting and/or several sets of conven- 
tional PCR. Although Southern blotting is indispensable 
for evaluating mtDNA rearrangements, long PCR provides 
a rapid screen for large mtDNA deletions in mitochon- 
drial diseases.

POSTINFECTIOUS DEMYELINATING 
POLYNEUROPATHY MIMICKING 
MYASTHENIA GRAVIS 
Ocular muscles are affected first in about half of the cases 
of myasthenia gravis resulting in fluctuating ptosis and 
diplopia. The fluctuating nature of myasthenic weakness 
is unlikely in any other disorder. The Guillain-BarrC syn- 
drome can cause ocular motor nerve paresis.' 
This report describes a patient who developed fluctuat- 
ing ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, and fatigue mimicking my- 
asthenia gravis in whom the neurophysiological investiga- 
tions showed a demyelinating polyneuropathy and 
increased orbicularis oculi muscle jitter. 
A 47-year-old man was referred for evaluation of bilat- 
eral ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, and fatigue. The patient 
was in excellent health until 2 weeks before, when he had 
fever, muscle tenderness and tiredness for some days. One 
week later he noticed increased tiredness with the custom- 
ary daily activities. Another week later he had diplopia, 
bilateral ptosis, and difficulty chewing and swallowing at 
the end of meals. All these symptoms were clearly improved 
by rest and worsened with prolonged activity and at the 
end of the day. On neurologic examination the patient 
had bilateral ptosis and marked limitation of all ocular 
movements in both eves with normal Dhotomotor reflexes.
